ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's foreign ministry said Wednesday that it has lodged a "strong" protest with the U.S. ambassador over missile attacks conducted on Pakistani soil by unmanned drones. The aftermath of a suspected U.S. drone attack on a building in North Waziristan. The ministry said it summoned Ambassador Anne Patterson to underscore that such attacks violate Pakistan's sovereignty and should be stopped immediately. A statement from the ministry said Patterson was also told that the attacks have cost lives and undermined public support for Pakistan's counter terrorism efforts. The ministry lodged its protests three days after a missile strike from a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Pakistan has repeatedly raised objections to foreign nations violating its sovereignty to pursue terrorists. A U.S. ground operation in September that left several civilians dead rankled relations between the two countries. Last week, Pakistan's parliament passed a resolution that condemned any incursion on Pakistani soil by foreign forces. The resolution called for a review of the country's national security strategy and said the government needs to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ministry said it handed Patterson a copy of the resolution. The U.S. and NATO, which have troops in Afghanistan, have been seeking a way to effectively battle militants who launch attacks from Pakistan's swath of tribal areas along the border. They have become frustrated with Islamabad over the years, saying it is not being proactive enough against militants -- a claim Pakistan denies. The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from drones, which are controlled remotely. In another development, suspected Taliban militants kidnapped three government officials from an administrative office in Pakistan's tribal region Wednesday, officials said. The militants abducted two employees and a security guard from the Ambar district in Mohmand Agency. Mohmand is in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where U.S. and Pakistani officials have reported a presence of militants. Earlier in the day, militants tried unsuccessfully to take control of a school in Mohmand and abduct about 100 students, authorities said. A shootout with Frontier Corps followed, in which one militant was killed and another arrested. The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary force which uses recruits from Pakistan's tribal areas and is overseen by Pakistani army officers. Also Wednesday, a suicide car bomber detonated explosives outside a police checkpoint in northwest Pakistan, killing two security personnel, officials said. The Wednesday afternoon attack in the Bannu district of the North West Frontier Province also wounded a dozen people, military sources said. The bomber targeted a check point near a military hospital, said the sources who did not want their names revealed because they are not authorized to speak to the media. CNN's Reza Sayah and journalist Janullah Hashimzada contributed to this report .

In an official statement, the ministry noted that Patterson was informed of how these strikes have resulted in the loss of human life while severely undermining public support for Pakistan’s broader counterterrorism initiatives. 

The diplomatic protest follows three days after a suspected U.S. drone strike on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Relations between the two nations were previously strained in September following a U.S. ground operation that resulted in several civilian casualties.

Last week, Pakistan’s parliament adopted a resolution condemning any incursion on national soil by foreign military forces. The resolution called for a comprehensive review of the country’s national security strategy, asserting the government's duty to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ministry confirmed that a copy of this resolution was delivered to Ambassador Patterson.

U.S. and NATO coalition forces in Afghanistan have long sought effective measures to combat militants launching cross-border attacks from Pakistan’s semi-autonomous tribal belt. Over the years, Western allies have expressed growing frustration with Islamabad, accusing it of failing to act proactively against insurgent groups—a charge Pakistan firmly denies. The United States remains the sole power operating in the region known to possess remotely piloted drones capable of executing targeted missile strikes.

In a separate development on Wednesday, suspected Taliban militants abducted three government personnel from an administrative facility in Pakistan’s tribal region. According to officials, the insurgents seized two employees and a security guard in the Ambar district of the Mohmand Agency—a territory within the Federally Administered Tribal Areas where both U.S. and Pakistani authorities acknowledge a strong militant presence.

Earlier that day, authorities reported that militants launched an unsuccessful attempt to storm a school in Mohmand and abduct approximately 100 students. The assault triggered a gunbattle with the Frontier Corps—a paramilitary force recruited from local tribal populations and led by Pakistani army officers—resulting in one militant being killed and another taken into custody.

Elsewhere in northwestern Pakistan on Wednesday afternoon, a suicide car bomber detonated explosives outside a security checkpoint, killing two personnel and wounding 12 others. **ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday formally summoned the United States Ambassador to lodge a strong protest over recent US drone strikes in the country’s northwestern border region, characterizing the operations as an unacceptable violation of national sovereignty and international law.

According to an official statement released by the Foreign Office, Foreign Secretary Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry met with US Ambassador Donald Blome in Islamabad to deliver a formal diplomatic protest, known as a *demarche*. 

During the high-level meeting, Pakistani officials expressed deep concern over the strikes, which took place near the Afghan border, targeting suspected militant hideouts. Islamabad urged Washington to immediately cease unilateral military actions within Pakistani territory.

"The Foreign Secretary conveyed Pakistan's strong stance that such drone strikes represent a clear breach of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity," the Foreign Office statement read. "It was emphasized that these unilateral actions are counterproductive, undermine mutual trust, and disregard the sacrifices made by Pakistan's security forces in combating terrorism."

Pakistani officials further argued that the strikes complicate local counterterrorism efforts and inflame anti-American sentiment among the civilian population, particularly in the affected tribal districts where civilian casualties remain a persistent concern.

The diplomatic rebuke follows a recent increase in tensions along the porous Durand Line, where US intelligence agencies have periodically used unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to target high-value commanders of the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) and foreign fighter networks. 

While Washington has historically viewed drone strikes as a necessary and effective tool to eliminate terrorists seeking safe haven in the remote border regions, Pakistan insists that any counterterrorism operations within its borders must be conducted exclusively by its own armed forces or through shared intelligence.

In a brief statement, a spokesperson for the US Embassy in Islamabad acknowledged the meeting at the Foreign Office, describing the discussions as "candid and professional."

"We do not comment on specific intelligence or operational matters," the embassy spokesperson said. "However, the United States remains committed to working with Pakistan in a shared effort to defeat terrorist threats that endanger both our nations and regional security."

The incident highlights the long-standing friction in US-Pakistan relations over counterterrorism strategy. Despite ongoing security dialogue and trade cooperation, the issue of airspace violations remains a flashpoint for Islamabad's civilian and military leadership.

Foreign Office sources indicated that Pakistan may raise the issue at upcoming United Nations forums if the unilateral strikes continue, warning that further incidents could force a re-evaluation of bilateral security coordination along the border.

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)** — Diplomatic relations between Washington and Islamabad reached a perilous new low Friday as Pakistan formally summoned U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson to protest a escalating campaign of American drone strikes along the rugged Afghan border.

The high-level diplomatic rebuke followed a deadly overnight missile strike in North Waziristan and coincided with a day of escalating violence across the region, highlighting the deepening strain on the U.S.-Pakistan counterterrorism alliance.

Pakistani Foreign Secretary Salman Bashir delivered a "strong protest" directly to Patterson at the Foreign Ministry in Islamabad, demanding an immediate end to the cross-border strikes, which Pakistani officials warn are undermining public support for their own military operations against Taliban and al Qaeda militants.

"It was underscored to the U.S. Ambassador that these attacks are unacceptable," the Pakistani Foreign Ministry said in a statement released shortly after the meeting. "They constitute a violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and undermine our public support for the war against extremism."

Patterson’s summoning represents one of the most explicit public rifts between the anti-terror partners since the U.S. dramatically stepped up its covert CIA-led drone program in Pakistan’s semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) earlier this year.

### A Formal Mandate Against Strikes

The diplomatic confrontation comes just weeks after Pakistan’s parliament unanimously passed a landmark resolution demanding an end to unilateral foreign military action on Pakistani soil. 

The 14-point resolution, passed following a rare closed-door briefing by military commanders, called for a re-evaluation of Pakistan's role in the U.S.-led "War on Terror" and insisted that national sovereignty be respected.

"The nation stands united against these incursions," said Defense Minister Ahmad Mukhtar following the parliamentary vote. "We cannot allow our territory to be used as a battlefield by outside forces without our consent."

While Washington views the lawless border region—particularly North and South Waziristan—as a safe haven for al Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden and Taliban fighters orchestrating attacks against U.S. troops in Afghanistan, Islamabad argues the civilian casualties caused by the strikes are fueling radicalization and destabilizing the country's fragile civilian government.

Officially, U.S. policy prohibits commenting on covert CIA operations, but American defense officials have privately expressed frustration over what they view as Islamabad’s reluctance or inability to clear out high-value militant targets in Waziristan.

### Chaos on the Ground

The diplomatic showdown coincided with a chaotic day of violence that underscored the fragile security situation across Pakistan.

* **Missile Strike in North Waziristan:** Local intelligence officials reported that a suspected U.S. unmanned aircraft fired two Hellfire missiles into a compound near Miramshah, the main town in North Waziristan, killing at least 12 people. Officials said several foreign fighters were believed to be among the dead, though civilian casualties were also reported.
* **NATO Supply Lines Attack:** In a dramatic show of force, dozens of heavily armed Taliban militants ambushed a convoy carrying vital supplies for U.S. and NATO forces near the Khyber Pass. Militants hijacked more than a dozen trucks carrying military vehicles and logistics equipment, temporarily forcing the closure of the primary trade and supply route linking Pakistan to Afghanistan.
* **Clashes in Bajaur:** To the north, heavy fighting broke out between Pakistani security forces and militants in the Bajaur tribal agency. Military spokesman Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas confirmed that army gunships targeted insurgent hideouts, leaving at least 15 suspected militants dead following an ambush on a military checkpoint earlier in the morning.

### A Tightrope for Washington and Islamabad

The rising friction poses a major challenge for the newly elected Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari, who is struggling to balance a desperate need for U.S. financial aid with fierce anti-American sentiment at home.

The tension also casts a long shadow over Washington, where President-elect Barack Obama is preparing to take office. Obama has previously signaled a willingness to strike high-value al Qaeda targets inside Pakistan if Islamabad fails to act, a stance that has raised alarms among Pakistani military officials.

As Patterson left the Foreign Ministry on Friday, U.S. Embassy officials in Islamabad maintained that Washington remains committed to working alongside Pakistan, but emphasized that combating the shared threat of terrorism remains the top priority.

Whether that diplomatic rhetoric can survive the mounting pressure on the ground in Waziristan, however, remains uncertain.

Pakistan’s civil and military leadership delivered a stern warning today against foreign border incursions, declaring that unilateral cross-border strikes severely undermine national sovereignty, even as domestic security forces battle intensifying militant violence across the unrest-racked Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA).

Speaking following a high-level national security briefing in the capital, Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gillani reiterated that Pakistan will not tolerate violations of its territorial integrity. The government's sharp rhetoric comes in the wake of a fresh wave of suspected U.S. CIA drone strikes targeting alleged al-Qaeda and Taliban hideouts in North and South Waziristan, as well as lingering fury over last month’s unprecedented ground raid by foreign forces in South Waziristan.

"The war on terror cannot be fought at the cost of our national self-respect," Gillani told reporters in Islamabad. "Unilateral actions within our borders are counterproductive and alienate the very public support needed to defeat extremists."

Army Chief Gen. Ashfaq Parvez Kayani reinforced the civilian government’s position, asserting that the defense of Pakistan’s borders remains the sole prerogative of the armed forces. Senior defense officials warned that persistent violations could jeopardize cooperation along the Afghan border and imperil vital NATO supply routes transiting through the Khyber Pass.

The diplomatic standoff with Washington comes as Pakistan’s military engages in some of its heaviest fighting to date inside FATA. In the northern Bajaur Agency, Pakistani troops backed by attack helicopters and artillery pressed forward today in Operation *Sherdil*, attempting to dislodge Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) fighters from strategic strongholds. 

According to military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas, security forces have killed dozens of insurgents over the past 48 hours in Bajaur and neighboring Swat. However, local officials report a severe humanitarian crisis unfolding, with an estimated 200,000 civilians displaced by the heavy shelling and ground combat. 

Militant backlash has been swift and bloody. Following the catastrophic suicide bombing of the Marriott Hotel in Islamabad late last month—an attack that shattered any sense of safety in the capital—militants have launched a series of retaliatory strikes against security checkpoints, police convoys, and anti-Taliban tribal elders across the northwest. 

In Parliament today, lawmakers from across the political spectrum began a rare, closed-door joint session to deliberate on the country’s security strategy. Opposition leaders demanded a firm deadline for the cessation of foreign air strikes, while government ministers sought to build national consensus around the campaign against homegrown militancy.

As the new administration of President Asif Ali Zardari struggles with a looming economic crisis, it faces an increasingly perilous balancing act: convincing a skeptical domestic public that the fight against extremism in FATA is Pakistan's own war, while attempting to halt armed incursions by the very foreign ally funding its military operations.

counterfactuals.output:
**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)** — For years, the skies above Pakistan’s rugged northwestern frontier were defined by a relentless, high-pitched hum. To the US intelligence community, the sound belonged to unmanned Predator and Reaper drones—the ultimate precision weapon in a global war on terror. But to the citizens and military leadership of Pakistan, that sound was a constant, buzzing reminder of compromised national sovereignty.

The fraught relationship between Washington and Islamabad—a marriage of geopolitical convenience forged in the aftermath of September 11—has faced many trials. Yet few issues have inflamed tensions as deeply as the clandestine US drone program and the rampant local militancy that devoured regions like the Mohmand Agency and the gateway city of Bannu.

As Washington prioritized the neutralization of high-value Al-Qaeda and Taliban targets, Pakistan found itself trapped in a double-bind: caught between the crossfire of American Hellfire missiles from above and a violent, local militant insurgency on the ground.

---

### Mohmand Agency: Ground Zero for Sovereignty Claims

In the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA)—now integrated into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province—the Mohmand Agency long served as a crucial battlefield. Bordering Afghanistan’s Nangarhar province, the agency's treacherous terrain made it an ideal sanctuary for foreign fighters, Al-Qaeda operatives, and factions of the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

For the CIA, Mohmand was a primary target zone. However, for Islamabad, unilateral US strikes in the region represented an intolerable breach of international law and territorial integrity. 

"Every time a drone crosses into Pakistani airspace without authorization, it is not just a tactical operation; it is an assault on our nation's sovereignty," said a senior Pakistani defense official, speaking to CNN on condition of anonymity. "You cannot build a partnership when one side acts as judge, jury, and executioner on the other’s sovereign land."

The friction reached boiling points following strikes that resulted in collateral damage. Local tribal elders in Mohmand frequently reported that civilian casualties were far higher than Washington acknowledged, fueling deep anti-American sentiment among a population already traumatized by militant violence. 

The outrage in Mohmand was not merely political; it was existential. Local residents described living in a state of perpetual anxiety under the unblinking eye of American drones. 

"We never knew when the sky would explode," recalled Malik Janan, a tribal elder from Mohmand, speaking via a local interpreter. "The Taliban terrorized us on the roads, and the drones terrorized us from above. We were hostages in our own homes."

---

### Bannu: The Gateway Under Siege

While Mohmand faced the brunt of aerial warfare, further south lies Bannu—a strategic district serving as the eastern gateway to North Waziristan. Bannu became a focal point for the complex web of local militancy that threatened to destabilize the Pakistani state from within.

Unlike the semi-autonomous tribal agencies, Bannu is a settled district. Yet, as the Pakistani military launched successive offensives to clear militants from neighboring Waziristan, Bannu became a cauldron of violence. It suffered devastating suicide attacks, complex ambushes, and high-profile militant operations—including a massive 2012 Taliban jailbreak that freed over 300 inmates.

The instability in Bannu highlighted Pakistan's core counter-argument to Washington: that US unilateral strikes were counterproductive, driving aggrieved locals into the arms of extremist groups like the TTP. 

Pakistani officials argued that while the US focused narrowly on cross-border targets threatening Western troops in Afghanistan, remote drone strikes in and around regions like Bannu undermined Pakistan’s own domestic counterterrorism strategies.

"The US drone strikes were a recruiter’s dream for the TTP," explained Maleeha Lodhi, a former Pakistani ambassador to the US and the UN. "Every civilian casualty, every uncoordinated strike created a new wave of militants, complicating the Pakistan military's effort to secure districts like Bannu."

---

### Washington’s Dilemma: Trust Deficit and Counterterrorism Urgency

From the perspective of Capitol Hill and the Pentagon, the calculus looked drastically different. American officials long harbored deep distrust toward Pakistan’s security apparatus, accusing elements within Islamabad of playing a "double game"—targeting militants that threatened the Pakistani state while harboring groups like the Haqqani Network that attacked US forces in Afghanistan.

For Washington, remote drone strikes were viewed as the only viable mechanism to strike time-sensitive targets in areas where the Pakistani military was either unable or unwilling to act. 

"We could not allow terrorists who were actively planning attacks against American soldiers to sit comfortably in safe havens," a former senior US intelligence official told CNN. "Where sovereignty is used as a shield to protect terrorists, the dynamic becomes incredibly complex. The drone program was designed to fill a lethal vacuum."

This fundamental trust deficit created a vicious cycle. The more the US struck targets unilaterally in Mohmand and the tribal belt, the more Pakistan protested the infringement on its sovereignty. The more Pakistan protested, the more Washington questioned Islamabad's commitment to the broader war on terror.

---

### The Legacy of a Shadow War

The intensity of the drone campaign has waned significantly in recent years, superseded by geopolitical shifts, the US withdrawal from Afghanistan, and changes in military doctrine. Furthermore, Pakistan’s military operations, such as *Zarb-e-Azb*, eventually reasserted state control over volatile zones like Mohmand and Bannu, albeit at a heavy human and economic cost.

Yet, the scar tissue from this era remains visible in US-Pakistan relations today. 

The debate over drone strikes in Mohmand and the spillover violence in Bannu fundamentally reshaped how the Pakistani public views Washington. It catalyzed a populist political shift within Pakistan, empowering political figures who built platforms on standing up to American dominance and demanding respect for national sovereignty.

Today, the bilateral relationship is cooler, stripped of the lofty language of strategic partnership, and reduced to a pragmatic, transactional dynamic.

"The shadow of the drone war still hangs over the relationship," said Dr. Rifaat Hussain, a Islamabad-based security analyst. "It taught Pakistan that strategic alignment with a superpower can come at the cost of your own domestic peace and sovereignty. That is a lesson Islamabad is unlikely to ever forget."

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)** — Pakistan has lodged a formal protest with U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson over ongoing American drone strikes in the country’s northwest, as a fresh wave of violent attacks—including a suicide bombing and high-profile kidnappings—continues to grip the region.

Pakistani foreign ministry officials summoned Patterson to express "deep concern" over the covert U.S. missile strikes targeting militant hideouts in North Waziristan, part of the semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) bordering Afghanistan.

Islamabad argued that the unmanned aerial strikes violate Pakistani sovereignty and are counterproductive to the government's efforts to win local support against extremism.

"The government of Pakistan has repeatedly conveyed that such attacks are a violation of our sovereignty and territorial integrity," a Pakistani senior foreign official said in a statement. "They fuel anti-American sentiment and complicate our military's strategy to stabilize the border regions."

Despite public protests from Pakistani leaders, Washington considers the CIA-led drone program a crucial tool in dismantling Al-Qaeda and Taliban networks operating in North Waziristan, an area long regarded as a launchpad for attacks against coalition forces in Afghanistan. U.S. officials rarely comment publicly on specific drone operations, but privately maintain that the strikes are precise and necessary to eliminate high-value targets.

The diplomatic friction comes amid deteriorating security across northwestern Pakistan, highlighting the government’s struggle to control militant groups.

In the city of Bannu, located near the entrance to North Waziristan, a suicide bomber detonated a vehicle packed with explosives near a security checkpoint, killing several police officers and injuring dozens of civilians, local police reported. The Pakistani Taliban claimed responsibility for the blast, calling it retaliation for military operations and drone strikes in the tribal region.

Further north, in the Mohmand Agency, security forces were carrying out search operations following a series of kidnappings targeting government workers and local tribal elders. Militants in Mohmand have increasingly turned to abductions and intimidation to enforce their influence and pressure the Pakistani military into backing off its localized offensives.

The complex security landscape puts immense pressure on the relationship between Washington and Islamabad. While the U.S. continues to press Pakistan for a full-scale military campaign against foreign fighters in North Waziristan, Pakistani officials maintain that their forces are already stretched thin dealing with domestic insurgencies, as evidenced by the violence in Bannu and Mohmand. 

U.S. Embassy officials confirmed Ambassador Patterson met with Pakistani authorities to discuss ongoing bilateral cooperation and security concerns, though specific details of the meeting were not disclosed.
